Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

schema.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
schema.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

schema.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
schema.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. **IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. # Case Study: Moving the Fast Session From Thursday to Friday at Kentucky

**What it is** — Morris describes one program's in-season change (QLdbKUiNadg [16:05], [16:36]).
- **Before:** Monday to Wednesday practice, Thursday the faster practice, Friday a complete walkthrough, Saturday game. With an evening Saturday game that left "48 hours potentially 72 hours" with little central-nervous-system or bioenergetic stimulus, and athletes "ended up coming out flat" (QLdbKUiNadg [16:36]).
- **Change:** a "fast Friday", keeping intensity on Friday while volume stays low.
- **Reported effect:** "our readiness will go you know through the roof both subjectively and objectively on game day"; the heart rate variability device ("mega wave", caption spelling) had shifted more parasympathetic under the old pattern, and subjective wellness rose on Saturday after the flip (QLdbKUiNadg [16:05], [16:36], [17:07]).
- **Measures:** wellness questionnaires plus a heart rate variability wearable, with the explicit caveat that heart rate variability gives "good things and bad things" (QLdbKUiNadg [16:05]).
- **Linemen detail:** linemen "don't do anything on Fridays" and the Friday drop is their lowest day, so they need the stimulation as much as the skill players (QLdbKUiNadg [13:58]). Skill players target about 75% of game high-speed distance in the week (QLdbKUiNadg [13:27]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that a long gap with no stimulation leaves the nervous system and energy systems flat for the game (QLdbKUiNadg [16:36]). He gives no data or test of that mechanism. Inference: it could also be that the athletes simply feel better with a familiar-intensity day, which the talk cannot separate.

**When to apply** — As an option to examine for evening or late-kickoff games where hard work ends three days out. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q15) describes Baylor's game week as Sunday off, Monday heavy lift, Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice with a lighter lift Wednesday, and "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game". Inference: the rule of ending hard work 72 hours out and the Fast Friday pattern are different designs, and this talk cannot decide between them. Eric's baseline: Eric's own SportSmith writing states that subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use because athletes learned to game them (`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`), so the subjective half of this evidence is the half he has distrusted.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one team's own change, no control, no numbers shown for the readiness changes, and no result on performance or injury. The speaker reports mixed value of heart rate variability. Wellness scores are subjective. Do not cite as evidence that Friday intensity improves game performance. Do not copy it into a Baylor week without Athletic Performance and the head coach, because it conflicts with the 72-hour rule above.

**Example** — The talk's own sequence: Thursday fast day plus Friday walkthrough replaced by Friday fast day, then readiness read from wellness and heart rate variability on Saturday (QLdbKUiNadg [16:05], [16:36]).

**Related** — [[claim--alactic-detraining-if-stimulated-only-on-game-day]], [[heuristic--hold-volume-raise-intensity-trim-low-value-periods]]; existing library: [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] and [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] (Issurin; the same logic of cutting volume while keeping maximal-speed and specific work before competition).

# Usage Bias: A Model Can Undervalue a Passer on a Run-Heavy Team, and a Pass Rusher Who Forces Runs

**What it is** — Paul Sabin names the main deficiency of his model: a quarterback who is very good at passing but whose coach does not use him that way (his example is Russell Wilson) may not show up as high as he should (oZsFyPGij0U [16:28]). He raises the mirror case on defense, Aaron Donald, typically considered the best defensive player. Against the pass his win rates are "so much better than everyone else it's not even on the chart," but against the run he is "not that great," and teams can usually run more effectively with him on the field (oZsFyPGij0U [16:28], [16:58]). Sabin's argument for Donald's value is that you would rather force a team to run, since running is less efficient (oZsFyPGij0U [16:58]). His planned fix is separate run and pass models next season, so players are not hurt by how they are used (oZsFyPGij0U [16:28], [16:58]). He also mentions Derrick Henry as roughly a top-10 impact player going into the playoffs (oZsFyPGij0U [15:58]). In recent NFL seasons the model's top players were Patrick Mahomes and Lamar Jackson, as spoken (oZsFyPGij0U [15:58]).

**Why it works** — Not a mechanism claim. The speaker's account is that a single value number pools run and pass plays, so a player whose strength lies on one side is graded on the play mix his coach chooses (oZsFyPGij0U [16:28]). The Donald point (forcing less efficient plays) is the speaker's assertion with no figures given.

**When to apply** — As a standing question when reading any single-number player grade: what is the player's usage, and what would the grade be if the coach called the plays differently? Inference: PFF-style grades and snap-based values at Baylor have the same exposure to play-calling mix. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: these are two named examples and a stated plan, with no numbers shown and no tested fix. The Donald claim about run-defense performance is a recollection ("teams usually can run more effectively when he's on the field"), not data in the talk. One case does not show how large the bias is across positions. The planned run and pass split was not built at the time of the talk, so no result exists.

**Example** — The speaker's own, above: Wilson (strong passer, run-heavy team) and Donald (elite pass rusher, weaker against the run) are the two illustrations of usage and play-type confounding.

**Related** — [[framework--position-variance-and-informative-priors-in-football-plus-minus]]; [[heuristic--separate-predictive-and-descriptive-versions-of-a-player-value-model]].

# If the Alactic System Is Stimulated Only on Saturday, It May Detrain: A Five-to-Eight-Day Rule of Thumb

**What it is** — Morris says that "from a physiologist standpoint" an energy system responsible for alactic power is lost if it is not stimulated "every five to eight days", so a lineman who only does game-like work on Saturday "was potentially detraining across the season" (QLdbKUiNadg [08:47]). He classifies the lineman's work as alactic: efforts of about 8 seconds, "anything less than ten all-out", repeated, with a work-to-rest ratio of about 1 to 3.75 (QLdbKUiNadg [10:50], [11:21]). The assertion is stated as a general fact with no citation.

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and no source for the five-to-eight-day figure. Inference: it is a detraining (loss of a trained quality without re-exposure) argument, and it sits in the same range as Issurin's residual duration for maximum speed (alactic), 5 ± 3 days, in the existing library entry below. Issurin's table is about a different population and different quality (maximal speed), so this is a similarity, not a confirmation.

**When to apply** — As a planning prompt: check when, in the week, each position group gets its most game-like, brief, all-out exposure. Inference: reporting "top quarter versus bottom quarter" odds is the kind of statement a coach can use to decide where to look.
claim--sleep-restriction-lowered-testosterone-by-10-to-12-percent.md:21:**When to apply** — As background for why sleep is mentioned alongside recovery and hormones, never as a clinical test. Inference: a first pass is to compare a model with the prior-load ratio alone against the same model plus today's planned session load. The speaker notes the approach needs "a fair bit of statistical" skill and that much of the original literature came from people whose background was not statistical (TIRINmtZOu0 [25:11], [25:41]). Eric's baseline (explicit, `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`): "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data." Inference: a before-and-after check of a candidate Baylor measure against a later outcome (a coach rating, an availability record) is a cheap way to meet that rule, with the outcome chosen first.

Inference: granting the coach's grain of truth fits that stance, because the eye is treated as a valid pointer. Inference: strength staff who write coach-facing reports can use the same sequence (belief, grain of truth, data, replacement mechanism).
framework--markov-decision-process-advantage-function-valuation.md:17:**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, frames basketball as a Markov decision process: a current state, an action taken, a stochastic transition, and an immediate reward measured both in expected points and in change in win probability (JjeFktc4QLM [04:05]). The key quantity is an advantage function: the expected value of an action beyond the baseline state expectation, which makes the valuation context-aware (JjeFktc4QLM [04:35]). Credit is split in two ways.

framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program.md:30:Eric's baseline: smooth, gradual progression is treated as protective and abrupt changes as an injury-risk driver (Inferred, transcript and slides, speaker unconfirmed, course team position); in-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (Inferred, transcript and shared slides, not claimed in interview). # A failed attempt to prove that curveballs are more dangerous than fastballs

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig says ASMI had advised for years not to throw curveballs until the growth plates close ("don't throw curve balls until you're old enough to shave") and ran studies to prove it (AgouMNTeyo4 [38:40], [39:11]). The result went the other way:

- Field: in the 10-year cohort of about 500 youth pitchers, those who started throwing curveballs younger were not the ones who got hurt (AgouMNTeyo4 [40:12]).

On pitch type, his group has studied fastballs, curveballs, changeups and sliders: fastballs, curveballs and sliders are stressful, changeups less so; split-fingered fastballs were not studied (AgouMNTeyo4 [53:02]).

371	
372	**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, tests how well the model predicts games on out-of-sample data, against a Vegas line benchmark. He reports that the Vegas line alone "is obviously the best, has the highest win prediction"; adding the deep RL Shapley values improves over the traditional metrics, and adding the synergy effects improves accuracy further, getting closer to the Vegas line (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42], [12:12]). He concludes the learned values "capture real forward-looking predictive signals" (JjeFktc4QLM [12:12]). The accuracy figures are shown only on a chart and are not stated in the captions, so no effect size can be cited here (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42]). The validation sums the players' Shapley values on the court to predict games, which a judge questioned (JjeFktc4QLM [13:13], [13:44]).

376	**When to apply** — As a model for how to validate a player-value metric: hold out data, compare against an existing predictive benchmark, and add the new metric to it rather than replacing it. Inference: a football grade or load metric could be tested the same way against a simple baseline on held-out games.

573	# Faster Pitches Put More Stress on the Elbow, Youth and Professional
574	
575	**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally's group at Henry Ford uses a wearable sleeve that detects stress and torque at the medial elbow, "right where the UCL is" (z_6M5r7031A [04:09]). He reports that, "study after study," the faster the pitch, the more elbow stress, and that this is pitch speed, not arm speed (z_6M5r7031A [04:39]). He says it holds for a 12-year-old youth pitcher and for a professional, and that it has been borne out in "numerous" independent studies from his group (z_6M5r7031A [04:39] to [05:10]). He contrasts it with older advice to avoid curveballs and off-speed pitches and "stick with straight fastballs" (z_6M5r7031A [04:39]).
576	
577	Related statements from the talk:
578	- Arm slot: studies of slot and release point exist, and "so far" slot has not shown increased elbow stress; this is the group's next stage (z_6M5r7031A [22:33]).
579	- Device limit: the sleeve relies on a throwing motion, so it cannot measure elbow stress in hitters (z_6M5r7031A [21:23]).
580	- Trend: average fastball velocity is climbing year over year, which he offers as one of two reasons the injury persists (z_6M5r7031A [04:09]).
581	
582	**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism. Inference: a faster release plausibly needs more force through the arm, so more load at the elbow is plausible, but the talk does not say so.
583	
584	**When to apply** — As background when a throwing sport (baseball, softball) asks whether to monitor throwing stress or velocity. Eric's baseline: a test or technology that "doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need" has no place (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q3). Inference: ask first what decision a sleeve or velocity number would change, then check validation (the talk does not describe any validation of the sleeve).
585	
586	**When NOT to apply** — The talk gives no effect sizes, sample sizes or ranges for these studies. The studies are the speaker's group's own, summarized aloud. The sleeve's validity is not discussed in the talk. It covers pitching only; he says UCL injury is essentially one position of one sport (z_6M5r7031A [21:54]). The slot finding is a preliminary "so far." Do not use it as a velocity limit for any athlete.
587	
588	**Example** — The speaker's own contrast: the old coaching rule was to avoid curveballs and change-ups because of elbow stress, while his group finds high-velocity fastballs also impart greater stress, in a 12-year-old and in a professional (z_6M5r7031A [04:39] to [05:10]).

16	# Inertial Movement Analysis May Describe Linemen Where GPS Distance Does Not
17	
18	**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") defines inertial movement analysis (IMA) as a count of movements in different directions (forward, backward, right, left and in between), built from accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer data and reported in three threshold bands (TbYgc6_qQzo [09:12]). His argument: GPS-type measures say a lot about outside players such as defensive backs and wide receivers, who produce much locomotor activity, but little about offensive and defensive linemen, because reliability falls when units record high-intensity activity in small spaces, "say below 20 meters," which is what linemen do (TbYgc6_qQzo [09:44]). 243	# A Lottery Based Only on Final Ranking Cannot Favor the Worst Team Without Some Incentive to Tank
244	
245	**What it is** — Evan Monroe (Stanford PhD student; caption spellings "Monroe" and "Munroe"; joint work with a fellow student the captions call "Martino") says the league's two objectives, backed out from its rule changes and statements, are (1) give the top pick to the lowest-ranked team with as high a probability as possible, subject to (2) removing incentives to tank (-6pe_zOKCig [04:39], [05:09]). Under a lottery that depends only on final win-loss ranking, "it's impossible" to favor the worst team at all without some incentive to tank (-6pe_zOKCig [08:44]). The options are to minimize the incentive by not favoring the worst team, or use a uniform lottery as in 1985 to 1989 (-6pe_zOKCig [08:44]). He quotes a hockey writer's line (caption spelling Greg Wyshynski) that if you do not want tanking you do not want the welfare mechanism that encourages it (-6pe_zOKCig [06:10], [06:41]). History he gives: before 1985 a coin flip between the two conference losers (worst team 50 percent), then an equal lottery for non-playoff teams that cut the worst team's chance to "between 11 and 14 percent" depending on team count (captions garbled), a 1990 figure the captions give as "70%" (looks garbled), 25 percent in 1994, and 14 percent in the most recent change (-6pe_zOKCig [03:09], [03:39], [04:09], [05:39]). He cites prior work showing statistically that teams with incentives to lose late in a season lose more (-6pe_zOKCig [06:41], [07:12]).
246	
247	**Why it works** — Speaker's argument (intuition, not the proof, which he says is in the paper): once a team is eliminated from the playoffs, its chance of making them is zero, so under a fixed lottery that favors bad teams, losing any game that affects its final ranking improves its draft odds (-6pe_zOKCig [10:49], [11:20]). The league sometimes penalizes egregious cases (-6pe_zOKCig [11:20]). The formal proof is not shown in the talk and was not checked here.
248	
249	**When to apply** — As a design test for any rule that rewards a poor result: if the reward depends only on the final outcome and favors the weakest, ask whether a rational participant gains by making the outcome worse. Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped after about a year because athletes learned the low-effort answers that looked clean but carried no signal (Explicit, SportSmith, 2026-02-19). Inference: that is a different mechanism (low effort, not deliberate losing) and the link to this result is by analogy only.
250	
251	**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the result is a theorem inside a model where teams value only the playoffs and the first pick, at fixed values, and only the first pick is allocated (-6pe_zOKCig [02:39], [09:46]). It covers league policy, not athlete monitoring. Real teams have broader goals, as the speaker says (-6pe_zOKCig [09:46]). His claim that tanking is "most intractable in the NBA" because key players matter so much is an assertion with no data shown (-6pe_zOKCig [02:39]).
252	
253	**Example** — The speaker's own: an eliminated team late in the season with a lottery that favors bad teams; every game affecting its ranking is one it gains by losing (-6pe_zOKCig [10:49], [11:20]).
254	
255	**Related** — [[principle--no-tanking-condition-benefit-of-winning-at-least-benefit-of-losing]]; [[framework--time-dependent-lottery-with-dynamically-frozen-odds]].

618	# If every concussion were caught and managed strictly, about one in five players would be out at any time
619	
620	**What it is** — A back-of-envelope availability model. The speaker, using the survey figure that about half of athletes have a concussion each year, takes a 50-person football team with half concussed (25 players) and 10 days out each: 250 days, "about 4% of playing days", "not completely disruptive" (npgdKKdJSww [12:12]). He then argues recovery is longer than 10 days (see the vulnerability-window entry) and reruns it at 60 days out: "21% of playing days", "one out of five athletes out at all times", about four of a football team's starters and one hockey starter at any moment, not counting repeat concussions (npgdKKdJSww [13:43], [14:14]). His conclusion is that either medical guidelines get much looser ("which won't happen") or the games change, starting with how much contact they contain (npgdKKdJSww [14:45], [22:58]).

16	# The Pressure Score Is Validated Only by Proxy and Does Not Assign Pressure to a Player
17	
18	**What it is** — Three limits the speaker states or concedes in the talk and Q&A.
19	
20	1. **Proxy evaluation only.** A continuous score is "hard to evaluate", so accuracy is measured through the maximum pressure on a passer compared with PFF hurry, hit and sack labels (1nt8hK2oYrE [10:54], [11:26]). No accuracy figure for the final score appears in the captions (F1 values 0.99 and 0.91 belong to the earlier identification and matchup stages, 1nt8hK2oYrE [07:47]).
21	2. **No player-level disentangling.** Asked how the model disentangles which player produced the pressure, he answers "we didn't actually try to disentangle which pressure is coming from which specific player" (1nt8hK2oYrE [21:40]); the target is "forgiving" and credits rushers inside a threshold area (1nt8hK2oYrE [22:12]), and he says they did not want to treat individual scores as each player's contribution to the whole (1nt8hK2oYrE [22:43]).
22	3. **No validation against a correlate.** Asked whether the score was checked against quarterback motion, he says no correlation analysis was done, and points to relative position, velocity and acceleration features instead (1nt8hK2oYrE [23:13], [23:43]).
23	
24	**Talk's own tension.** The sample plays credit individual players with high pressure scores (1nt8hK2oYrE [13:00], [14:04]) while the Q&A says the model does not separate whose pressure it is. The talk does not reconcile these. The summary file for this talk reads it the same way.

26	Also named: scheme and strategy not modeled (1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]), and complex position features not modeled (1nt8hK2oYrE [18:38]).

28	**Why it works** — Not applicable; this is a limits entry. The speaker gives no mechanism for the performance disparity he mentions (1nt8hK2oYrE [11:58]).

Inference: ask the same of any per-player number.

393	# Top and Bottom Test-Score Quartiles Were Rated Three to Four and a Half Times Apart by Coaches
394	
395	**What it is** — To make correlations of about 0.3 usable, the first speaker (caption spelling "Ken yuso") splits scores into high, medium and low; high and low each hold "about 25% of the sample", and the coaches' ratings (a scale of about seven points) fall into matching bands (40NV3_u9tYY [12:27], [12:59]). Reported results:
396	- **Intelligence:** low scorers were about three times more likely to be rated "poor performers or disappointments" than stars; high scorers about three times more likely to be rated stars than disappointments (40NV3_u9tYY [13:30]).
397	- **High intelligence scorers:** rated low by coaches 13% of the time, good to great 87% of the time (40NV3_u9tYY [14:01]).
398	- **Personality:** low scorers about four times as likely to be rated low as high; high scorers rated high about four and a half times as often; 91% of strong personality scorers rated good to great (40NV3_u9tYY [14:32], [15:02]).
399	- False positives and false negatives, "the misses", were "pretty low" for the top and bottom groups; the speaker says he is not showing the middle group (40NV3_u9tYY [14:01], [15:02]).
400	He notes he was "surprised that the coaches were pretty straightforward" in how they used the scale (40NV3_u9tYY [12:59]).
401	
402	**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond presenting the bands as a way to show what a correlation of this size looks like in a cut-score decision (40NV3_u9tYY [12:27], [14:01]). Inference: with about 0.3 correlation, tails separate more clearly than the middle, so band odds look stronger than the correlation alone suggests.
403	
404	**When to apply** — When explaining a modest correlation to a coach or director. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." Inference: reporting "top quarter versus bottom quarter" odds is the kind of statement a coach can use to decide where to look.
405	
406	**When NOT to apply** — The speaker states the middle half, where most decisions fall, was not shown. These odds are for a combine test and coach ratings, in the NFL, for players with at least a year of data; they are not injury or performance results. The bands compare the extremes, and 87% "good to great" is of those rated, with 70% team participation (40NV3_u9tYY [09:22]). No intervals or sample sizes for each band are given. Do not apply as a cut score for athletes: the speaker says the test is meant as an incremental data point (40NV3_u9tYY [06:17]).
407	
408	**Example** — The speaker's own: a high personality score met a "good to great" rating 91% of the time (40NV3_u9tYY [15:02]).

626	# Sleep Restriction Lowered Testosterone by 10 to 12% in Young College Students, the Speaker Says
627	
628	**What it is** — The speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says growth hormone is secreted in deep sleep and testosterone is secreted while sleeping (with another peak while awake) (J7smyg1Czik [05:40]). She describes an experiment in which young healthy college students had five fewer hours than eight in bed, and their testosterone levels fell by 10 to 12% (the captions read "increased... decreased", so the direction is inferred from the following sentence) (J7smyg1Czik [05:40], [06:12]). Normal aging loss is 1 to 2% per year, so she says a 20-year-old after a week of restriction would look like a 31-year-old (J7smyg1Czik [06:12]). She adds that sleep loss raises the hormones that break down muscle (J7smyg1Czik [06:42]).
629	
630	**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that the hormones are released in sleep, so less sleep means less of them. She names no study authors for any of these results. Inference: a reduction of 10 to 12% in a one-week laboratory restriction of young men says little about an athlete's day-to-day testosterone.
631	
632	**When to apply** — As background for why sleep is mentioned alongside recovery and hormones, never as a clinical test. Inference: the finding supports asking about sleep when an athlete reports poor recovery. Eric's baseline: nothing objective is tracked for recovery or sleep (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit); no hormone testing is in the baseline.
633	
634	**When NOT to apply** — Untested: unnamed studies, sample sizes and durations not stated, and the caption garble in the key sentence. Young healthy college students (the speaker does not say how many or of which sex) in laboratory conditions. Existing library: a 2026 review of testosterone in athletes notes that sleep loss and sleep-disordered breathing may contribute to impaired testosterone regulation, and that evidence for sleep extension or melatonin as testosterone-enhancing interventions is not established, so do not present this as a treatment effect. The "age 31" comparison is the speaker's illustration, not a finding she cites. Do not use this to interpret an athlete's own lab values.
635	
636	**Example** — The speaker's own: a 20-year-old player after a week of lost sleep, with testosterone like that of a 31-year-old (J7smyg1Czik [06:12]).
637	
638	**Related** — [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]; [[claim--sleep-hours-predicted-injury-in-high-school-athletes]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/lazarev-2026-testosterone-optimizing-strategies-in-athletes]] (partial tension on sleep as an intervention, not on the effect of loss).

15	
16	# Many MLB Pitchers Do Not Return to Prior Durability After UCL Reconstruction
17	
18	**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally (sports medicine orthopedic surgeon and Detroit Lions team physician, per the host, z_6M5r7031A [00:00]) reports public-data cohort results on ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) reconstruction, "Tommy John surgery," in Major League Baseball pitchers. The speaker says he was told early on that the surgery "works for everybody" (z_6M5r7031A [09:13]).
19	- **Cohort:** 150 MLB pitchers who had the surgery, of whom 140 were "established," defined as pitching in 10 or more games in a season (z_6M5r7031A [09:13]).
20	- **Not back:** 20% of the established pitchers never pitched in the majors again (z_6M5r7031A [09:13] to [09:43]).
21	- **Back, but reduced:** "one out of three" came back but never reached 10 games a year again, pitching one or two games (z_6M5r7031A [09:43]). The caption does not say whether the denominator is all 140 or only those who returned.
22	- **Those who returned:** a statistically significant decline in "numerous pitching metrics" (z_6M5r7031A [09:43] to [10:13]). The metrics and effect sizes are not named or shown.
23	- **Value curve:** wins above replacement (WAR) fell over the 3 years before surgery and took 3 years after return to reach the pre-surgery level. With 12 to 18 months to get back to the majors, he puts the full path at about four to four and a half years (z_6M5r7031A [10:13] to [10:43]).
24	- **Controls:** in Q&A he says the first data set used age-matched controls and the second was not controlled for starter versus reliever (z_6M5r7031A [18:19]). On recovery by age, the numbers were too small to separate, and the pattern looked like the natural trend with age (z_6M5r7031A [18:50]).
25	
26	**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for the post-surgery decline. He does say professional tears are usually attritional, a slow wearing down with pathology building up in the elbow (z_6M5r7031A [26:13]). Inference: a WAR decline that starts three years before surgery fits that account, but the talk does not link the two.
27	
28	**When to apply** — As a reality check on the idea that reconstruction restores a pitcher to prior form, and as an outside comparison when explaining return-to-play expectations for a throwing athlete. Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's stated role in return to performance is to supply information that supports Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine decisions, not to make the final decision (Explicit, Baylor Applied Performance Playbook p.6). Inference: the figures are context for those conversations, to be handled by Athletic Medicine.
29	
30	**When NOT to apply** — This is professional baseball pitching, "one position of one sport" by the speaker's own description (z_6M5r7031A [21:54]). Do not read it across to football, to college athletes, or to Baylor injury types. The period of the 150-pitcher cohort is not stated. The "one out of three" denominator is ambiguous in the captions. The second WAR analysis was uncontrolled (z_6M5r7031A [18:19]). The pitching metrics that declined are not named. This is one surgeon's group reporting public-data analyses, not a controlled comparison with non-operative care. Eric's baseline: the baseline holds no specific return-to-play criteria to compare against (Explicit principle, gap in criteria, Playbook p.6; a written protocol exists in the UE and LE rehab templates, interview Q4a, not yet read by Flint).
31	
32	**Example** — The speaker's own definition: an "established" pitcher is one with 10 or more games in a season, so "never returned" means never again at the major league level at all (z_6M5r7031A [09:13] to [09:43]). Inference: 20% of 140 is 28 pitchers; the speaker gives only the percentage.
33	
34	**Related** — [[claim--salary-cost-of-ucl-rehab-2004-2014]] (same speaker, same public-data approach). [[framework--expected-value-decision-analysis-for-treatment-choice]] (the model these outcomes would feed). Reciprocal-link suggestion: [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] in the Old Bull library (a single dramatic result, here surgery, should not settle a decision).

371	# Adjust Injury Models for the Load of the Session Itself
372	
373	**What it is** — The speakers' proposed fix is to include the actual load of the session in which an injury occurred, alongside any prior-load ratio (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]). Options they name: survival models, which look at when the athlete was injured and how intense the session was up to that moment; latent variable models that use the loads of other players in the same session who were not injured (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49], [18:19]); and, in the Q&A, predicting the upcoming session's load from the previous seven days and treating it as an unmeasured confounder (TIRINmtZOu0 [25:11]). They report that once session load was accounted for, ACWR went "from being highly significant to being non-significant" in all their cases (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:19], [18:49]). They also report that acute load alone gave the same results as the ratio, and that coupled and uncoupled denominators gave the same results (TIRINmtZOu0 [26:42]).
374	
375	**Why it works** — If session intensity is the confounder, holding it fixed removes the route through which the ratio looks predictive; see [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]. The speakers do not show the models, the adjusted effect sizes, or the confidence intervals ("in the paper", TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]), so the mechanism is described, not demonstrated, in the talk.
376	
377	**When to apply** — When building or auditing an injury model on load data with session-level records. Inference: a first pass is to compare a model with the prior-load ratio alone against the same model plus today's planned session load. The speaker notes the approach needs "a fair bit of statistical" skill and that much of the original literature came from people whose background was not statistical (TIRINmtZOu0 [25:11], [25:41]). Eric's baseline: there is no formal risk model, and sport science support exists for few teams ("we don't have sport science support for most teams", interview 2026-09-28, Q12 and Q28, Explicit); this would need dedicated analyst time.
378	
379	**When NOT to apply** — Untested here: significance vanishing is reported, with no effect sizes, sample size, injury counts or model specification. Significance loss with few injuries says little about whether a real effect exists, and the speakers say a richer multivariate model may still find a signal (TIRINmtZOu0 [23:35]). Requires session load for every player and session, including the injured one, which a speaker says is usually thrown out (see [[heuristic--keep-the-load-of-the-injured-session]]). Two teams, two sports.
380	
381	**Example** — Inference: for a non-contact hamstring injury in a Tuesday practice, the record would hold the Tuesday session's planned intensity next to the prior-week ratio; the model asks whether the ratio adds anything once Tuesday's intensity is in.
382	
383	**Related** — [[heuristic--keep-the-load-of-the-injured-session]]; [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]; [[framework--null-model-simulation-to-test-a-risk-metric]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]].

613	# Validate an Assessment Before Using It: Score Early, Rate Later, Correlate
614	
615	**What it is** — The first speaker (caption spelling "Ken yuso"; he thanks co-authors "Charles sheram" and Harold Goldstein, 40NV3_u9tYY [00:03]) describes a three-step validation of the NFL's one-hour psychological test. His background: industrial and organizational psychologists, "heavy litigation, employment discrimination" work, where "you have to demonstrate that what you're measuring actually is connected to some meaningful outcome" (40NV3_u9tYY [08:21], [08:52]). Design as reported:
616	- **Predictor:** the assessment taken at the combine before any NFL playing time; 1,500 player scores over three years, about 330 combine participants a year plus a "Super Regional" (40NV3_u9tYY [08:52]).
617	- **Criteria:** team coaches' ratings on about 24 dimensions after the player had been on the team at least a year, with about 70% participation across all 32 teams per year (40NV3_u9tYY [09:22], [09:54]); also on-field metrics (penalties per play, yards per penalty) and injuries (40NV3_u9tYY [16:35], [17:37]).
618	- **Sample:** about 500 players with performance data (40NV3_u9tYY [09:54]).
619	- **Results (decimal points are garbled in the captions: "0 28", "about3", "a0 29", "about 35"):** about 0.28 overall, about 0.3 for the cognitive composite, about 0.29 for the personality composite, about 0.35 combined (40NV3_u9tYY [10:24], [10:56], [11:26], [15:33]). He calls the correlations "uncorrected", "extremely conservative" and good for behavioral science (40NV3_u9tYY [10:24]).
620	He adds that "no test as a crystal ball" and that the test is meant as an addition to physical and skills measures (40NV3_u9tYY [11:57], [10:24]).
621	
622	**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the standard predictive validity logic: measure first, then check against what happens later (40NV3_u9tYY [09:54]: "a classic validation study"). The mechanism by which a trait score would produce coach ratings is not given. Inference: the key protection is that the predictor is collected before the outcome exists, which the speaker describes, though the talk does not say whether coaches saw the test results (see the limits below).
623	
624	**When to apply** — When deciding whether to add or keep a test. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." Eric's baseline (explicit, `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`): "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data." Inference: a before-and-after check of a candidate Baylor measure against a later outcome (a coach rating, an availability record) is a cheap way to meet that rule, with the outcome chosen first.
625	
626	**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is supported, not proven: the speakers report the method and correlations, but give no confidence intervals, no subgroup sizes and no position splits. The main criterion is coach opinion, not performance. The talk does not say whether coaches saw the test scores before rating (40NV3_u9tYY [09:22], per the summary's limits). The speakers run the assessment, so this is not an independent evaluation, and co-author Harold Goldstein was absent (40NV3_u9tYY [00:03]). Participation was "about 70%" (40NV3_u9tYY [09:22]), so non-response is possible, and the sample is rookies and early-career players only. Correlations near 0.3 explain about 9% of variance (Inference: arithmetic on r squared), so use them for broad sorting, not individual calls.
627	
628	**Example** — The speakers' own: the test scores taken at the combine against ratings given a year or more later for "learn the game readily", mental errors, decisions under stress, leadership, work ethic and similar dimensions (40NV3_u9tYY [10:56], [11:26]).
629	
630	**Related** — [[claim--score-bands-map-to-coach-rating-odds]], [[claim--decisions-under-stress-needs-ability-plus-stress-tolerance]], [[principle--add-standardized-psychological-data-as-increment-not-substitute]]; existing library: [[heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]] (Old Bull), and the research brief [[farrell-2024-beyond-the-box-score-using-psychological-metrics-to-forecast-nba-success]].

15	
16	# To Change a Prior Belief, Grant the Grain of Truth, Show the Data, and Replace the Story
17	
18	**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now"; director of basketball research for the Milwaukee Bucks, as he states at BJkCqf6Fj2w [00:30]) says the "meta point" of his talk is that "the way we talk about our statistical insights is a vital thing towards them actually being adopted" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [01:30]). His reasoning:
19	- Citing Kahneman and Tversky (caption spelling "conman tki"), he says the human mind is "really bad" at statistical information not attached to a narrative or a mechanism (BJkCqf6Fj2w [02:00]).
20	- People in sport have "very strong prior opinions", often based in fact; "it's not just enough to say well here's some stats that tell you you're wrong" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [02:30]).
21	- The aim is to give people "the permission" to accept a new narrative (BJkCqf6Fj2w [03:00]).
22	- His procedure, applied to four complaints about the three-point shot: state the belief, grant its "grain of truth" (many such narratives are "completely true" in part), show what the data say, then offer a better explanation of why (BJkCqf6Fj2w [03:30], [08:10]). For example, the same fact can be heard as teams "settling" for long jumpers or as using "the geometry of the court" because three is greater than two (BJkCqf6Fj2w [06:03]).
23	He ends by calling his account a theory and welcoming "better theories", with the goal to be "less wrong" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [21:22]).
24	
25	**Why it works** — Given by the speaker: a mechanism lets listeners replace the old picture, whereas numbers alone do not (BJkCqf6Fj2w [02:00], [02:30]). He supplies no test showing that framing changes adoption. Inference: this is a claim about communication practice from his experience, not a measured effect.
26	
27	**When to apply** — When a coach holds a strong belief the data contradict. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." Inference: granting the coach's grain of truth fits that stance, because the eye is treated as a valid pointer. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q28): "Strength staff will build it most likely; we don't have sport science support for most teams." Inference: strength staff who write coach-facing reports can use the same sequence (belief, grain of truth, data, replacement mechanism).
28	
29	**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the speaker's assertion from his experience and a literature reference, with no evidence of adoption results. His own caution is that the mechanisms in the talk are theory (BJkCqf6Fj2w [21:22]), and a story can persuade without being right: the fast-break explanation below is his hypothesis, not tested (BJkCqf6Fj2w [08:10]). Do not use a reframe to hide a weak finding; the order is data first, then the explanation. It also does not replace working with a coach who has already decided.
30	
31	**Example** — From the talk: "the NBA has become a jump shooting league" is answered by granting that teams take many jump shots, then showing the share beyond 10 feet was 55% in 1999 to 2000 and 55% the previous season (BJkCqf6Fj2w [04:32]).

341	
342	# Valuing actions with a Markov decision process and an advantage function
343	
344	**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, frames basketball as a Markov decision process: a current state, an action taken, a stochastic transition, and an immediate reward measured both in expected points and in change in win probability (JjeFktc4QLM [04:05]). The key quantity is an advantage function: the expected value of an action beyond the baseline state expectation, which makes the valuation context-aware (JjeFktc4QLM [04:35]). Credit is split in two ways.
345	- **On-ball offense** (shots, assists, turnovers): valued by action type, player role and game context (JjeFktc4QLM [04:35], [05:07]).
346	- **Defense and off-ball influence**: valued by presence and constraints, not individual actions, to capture deterrence unseen in box scores (JjeFktc4QLM [05:07]).
347	He positions it against three earlier families: box-score metrics (PER, win shares, box plus-minus: fixed weights, overweight scoring, weak on defense, no context), adjusted and regularized adjusted plus-minus (RAPM: regress possession outcomes on who is on the floor, but assume context-invariant contributions and miss synergy), and sequential models such as expected possession value (capture flow but struggle to credit players) (JjeFktc4QLM [01:01], [01:31], [02:02], [02:32]). The video description also names temporal-difference learning and a distributional win-probability model; the captions do not describe them. One caption spelling, "DRPM", appears for the model's name (JjeFktc4QLM [15:49]).
348	
349	**Why it works** — The speaker says deep reinforcement learning can combine the strength of sequential models (context and the flow of play) with player-level credit (JjeFktc4QLM [02:02], [02:32]). The captions give no training details, so how well the learned values are calibrated is not stated.
350	
351	**When to apply** — As a checklist for what a valuation model must handle: state, action, transition, reward, a baseline for "expected from this state", and a separate route for value that is not an action (defense, spacing). Inference: for football, ask the same questions of any grade or load number before comparing players. Eric's baseline: no direct position on valuation models (method-baseline.md).
352	
353	**When NOT to apply** — Untested for this audience: the captions show no model specification, no calibration and no uncertainty for player values, and predictive accuracy is shown only on a chart (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42]). It was built on about five seasons of NBA play-by-play (JjeFktc4QLM [16:21]); a football version needs its own state definition and a win-probability model, and none was shown. The defensive-value claims rest on the model with no independent check named.
354	
355	**Example** — The speaker's own: a made three as the action, with reward measured as expected points on the play plus change in win probability (JjeFktc4QLM [04:05]).
356	
357	**Related** — [[principle--identical-actions-carry-different-win-value-by-game-state]], [[framework--neural-shapley-credit-and-player-dropout]], [[claim--drl-shapley-predicts-games-better-than-box-metrics-but-not-vegas]].

690	# Pitch Smart: a three-part program of count limits, plain-language research and accurate surgery information
691	
692	**What it is** — John DeAngelo (MLB) describes how the league office turned a medical committee's research into a youth program. In 2014 the Commissioner's Office convened leading medical experts (the speaker names the orthopedist Dr Andrews and ASMI's research director, caption "dr. fly cigs", plus team physicians and researchers) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [06:52]). They told it that the single greatest factor was youth overuse and rest, and that "very modifiable" behaviors correlated with injury in youth; the best study followed youth pitchers for ten years and found 100 or more innings a year went with more serious arm injury (sHXuxj3-rbQ [07:22], [07:54]). GMs, coaches and players also said specializing early and playing year round with high single-game pitch counts raised risk (sHXuxj3-rbQ [08:24]).
693	
694	The program, with USA Baseball, launched in November 2014 (caption "pitch mark", "pitch smart", read here as Pitch Smart) (sHXuxj3-rbQ [08:54], [12:30]). Three parts (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:24], [09:55]):
695	- Pitch count limits and required rest guidelines from age 7 to 22, with allowed pitches rising by age and rest days rising with pitches thrown in a game; example: throw 50 pitches, wait two days before pitching again (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:24], [10:25]).
696	- Research synthesized into digestible information for players and coaches, so they understand why.
697	- Accurate information about Tommy John surgery.
698	
699	Adoption (sHXuxj3-rbQ [13:03], [13:33], [14:04], [14:36]): Little League already had guidelines; showcase circuits (caption "perfect game") and college summer leagues including the Cape Cod League comply; in 2014 Vermont was the only state with a pitch-count-based high school rule; in 2016 the National Federation of State High School Associations voted to require states to adopt a pitch-count and required-rest rule; in 2017 the speaker counts 44 or 46 states (the caption is ambiguous) with Connecticut and Massachusetts as holdouts. States do not all follow the Pitch Smart table exactly.
700	
701	**Why it works** — The speaker's logic is that the research already existed and the rest-after-a-count rule (the 50 pitches, two days example) is "a pretty intuitive concept" that had not been widely adopted (sHXuxj3-rbQ [09:24]). He gives no evidence that adoption reduced injuries. Inference: the program's contribution is distribution and compliance, not new evidence, which is how an overuse rule becomes a rule.
702	
703	**When to apply** — As a model for converting a research finding into an enforceable exposure rule: name an authority, set limits that scale by age and dose, publish the reasons, and recruit governing bodies. Inference: for Baylor, the equivalent is a written exposure rule a staff member can apply the same way each time.
704	
705	Eric's baseline: smooth, gradual progression is treated as protective and abrupt changes as an injury-risk driver (Inferred, transcript and slides, speaker unconfirmed, course team position); in-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (Inferred, transcript and shared slides, not claimed in interview). Inference: a pitch count with rest is a dose rule of that kind. The baseline holds no throwing or contact-exposure rule.
706	
707	**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `untested` because the talk shows no outcome for the program: the speaker said surgeries leveled off and did not claim the guidelines caused it (sHXuxj3-rbQ [14:36], [15:37]). He works for the league office and describes the league's own program. The age and pitch table is not reproduced in the transcript, so no specific limit can be cited from this talk. Youth baseball pitchers; do not transfer to football. The 2012 concussion speaker, discussing pitch counts, calls the age caps "clearly not based on much science" (npgdKKdJSww [17:19]), a caution on how much weight a count table can bear.
708	
709	**Example** — The speaker's own: the 2016 high school federation vote, from one state with a rule to nearly all (sHXuxj3-rbQ [13:33], [14:04], [14:36]).

16	# When the Athlete Creates His Own Context: Combine General and Specific Context Estimates
17	
18	**What it is** — In catch score, a panelist describes a "catch over predicted" residual: the model predicts a catch probability, and the receiver is credited the remainder if he catches it and debited the predicted probability if not (a 0.75 prediction and a catch is credited +0.25) (teg9SfzpMy0 [24:17], [24:48]). The problem that "almost killed" the project: the receiver creates the context himself (the move that got him open), so a model that adjusts for the field at ball arrival penalizes him for making the catch easy (teg9SfzpMy0 [24:48], [25:18]). The solution, described as a "Eureka moment":
19	- **General context ("expected" in their words):** coverage, route, depth, play action, slot alignment and distance from the sideline (teg9SfzpMy0 [25:49], [26:20]).
20	- **Specific context ("predicted"):** all the tracking positions at ball arrival, through a position-invariant convolutional neural network (teg9SfzpMy0 [23:47], [26:20]).
21	- **Combination:** both helped predict yards per route run, so catch score combines the two (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52]).
22	- Without the combination, contested-catch receivers would benefit from their inability to create separation (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52], [27:22]). The panel says completion probability over expected for quarterbacks cannot be turned around for receivers for the same reason (teg9SfzpMy0 [27:52], [28:23]).
23	
24	**Why it works** — The panel's reasoning is that the general estimate does not see the receiver's separation and the specific estimate does, so the pair brackets how hard the catch was relative to how he got there (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:20], [26:52]). They give no test showing that the combination removes the bias. Inference: the combination is a compromise, justified by predicting yards per route run (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52]), not by showing context was removed.
25	
26	**When to apply** — When an athlete's own action changes the conditions of the thing being graded. Inference: in a jump or sprint assessment, an athlete who changes his own start or setup alters the test condition, so the comparison should hold the conditions that he controls fixed, or be labeled.
27	
28	**When NOT to apply** — The captions give no quantities for either estimate or for the combined catch score, and the check against yards per route run is qualitative (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52]). `untested`. The data are NFL tracking data, x and y only (teg9SfzpMy0 [46:15]). A panelist adds YAC uses video-tracked ball placement as well as the dots (teg9SfzpMy0 [28:55]), so video charting is also part of the system. The metric is for fan content.
29	
30	**Example** — The panel's: Alan Robinson, Kenny Golladay and Terry McLaurin (caption spellings) as contested-catch receivers who would look best if the context credit weren't adjusted (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52], [27:22]).
31

291	# Moving an NFL Tracking Model to College: Adjust for Quality of Competition
292	
293	**What it is** — A questioner asked whether the approach carries over to college, "especially" the G4 and G5 schools (Group of Four, Group of Five; caption spellings) versus NFL results (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [12:05], [12:35]). Jenkins answers that it could apply to college and Power-4 data, because computer vision gives actual tracking data at the college level, and that "an important consideration" is to account more for competition differences, since "quality of competition is going to be important in college more than NFL" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [12:35]). He suggests it as extendable to other positions and sports (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [09:35]).
294	
295	**Why it works** — The speaker's reason is only that opponents differ more in quality in college. He shows no adjustment and no college results. Inference: if linemen face very different opponents, an unadjusted credit mixes player skill with opponent strength.
296	
297	**When to apply** — Before using any NFL-built model on Baylor or opponent data: ask the vendor how it adjusts for competition level, and whether the model was fit on college data. Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports Athletics Performance decisions and does not own the call (Eric-authored Playbook p.6, in method-baseline.md), so the practical step is to put this question to the vendor or the football staff's analyst before a number is shown to coaches.
298	
299	**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: the answer is a statement, with no college application in the talk. The speaker did not say what the adjustment would be or whether tracking quality at the college level matches the NFL's. The method is the speaker's own and he works at Sumer Sports. The question and answer concern pass blocking only, and he did not discuss any specific school or conference.
300	
301	**Example** — The Q&A exchange itself (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [12:05], [12:35]).
302

433	# Hold Total Load, Raise Intensity: Trim Low-Value Practice Periods and Ask for Full Speed in the Rest
434	
435	**What it is** — Asked whether there is evidence that raising practice workload changes game performance or fatigue, Morris answered with his approach, not evidence (QLdbKUiNadg [14:35], [15:05]):
436	- "maintain load", control load, "increase our intensity", and prefer shorter, more intense practices (QLdbKUiNadg [15:05]).
437	- "You can't increase the intensity and volume" together "because then you create massive amounts of fatigue"; wellness questionnaires help judge internal load next to external load (QLdbKUiNadg [15:35]).
438	- Camp example: in a three-hour practice a skill player may cover about 7,000 yards but "he's just gonna pace", at "1718 miles an hour" (caption; read as 17 to 18 mph in the summary). The quarterback's timing is then off when receivers move faster in a game (QLdbKUiNadg [15:05], [15:35]).
439	- With wide receivers, the compromise was to pull back seven-on-seven blitz-package periods where they were "just running routes for no reason", so they run full speed in the remaining seven-on-seven and team periods, with load unchanged (QLdbKUiNadg [18:08]).
440	- Target for skill players: about 75% of game high-speed distance during the week (QLdbKUiNadg [13:27]).
441	
442	**Why it works** — The speaker's explanation is that athletes pace themselves when practice is long, so the pace they learn is not the pace of the game (QLdbKUiNadg [15:05]). The claim that both volume and intensity cannot rise without fatigue is stated as fact without evidence (QLdbKUiNadg [15:35]). Inference: this is a restatement of constant-load, higher-intensity redistribution and relies on external load (GPS) staying equal while the mix changes.
443	
444	**When to apply** — In camp or in-season when practices run long and speed is low per period. Eric's baseline: the HHPR 5355 course material states the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21`), tagged Inferred (course-team speaker unconfirmed). Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q18): "I don't have the specific sets and reps." Inference: Morris's version adds the practical lever (cut low-value periods, name the intensity expected in the rest).
445	
446	**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the speaker's assertion and one camp example. The questioner asked for evidence and the answer gave his approach, with no outcome data (QLdbKUiNadg [14:35], [15:05]). The 17 to 18 mph figure is a caption problem and implausible as a sustained pace; do not quote it. The "75% of game high-speed distance" target is Kentucky's for skill players, not a validated number. Athlete and coach consent matters, as the speaker's own Eagles anecdote shows (see the related entry).
447	
448	**Example** — The wide-receiver compromise above: fewer seven-on-seven blitz-pack reps, full speed in the ones that remain, unchanged load (QLdbKUiNadg [18:08]).
449
