16	# Before Trying Conservative Care First, Price What Happens If It Fails
17	
18	**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally answers the obvious proposal, "why not just let everybody try non-operative treatment" first, with a question: what if it does not work? (z_6M5r7031A [14:45] to [15:15]). If the trial burns 3 months of rest, activity modification and physical therapy and the athlete still needs surgery, then instead of losing one season by operating at once, "you've now lost two" (z_6M5r7031A [15:15]). His numbers for the two branches: non-operative success of 40 to 80% depending on the case, at most a 3-month downtime (z_6M5r7031A [14:14] to [14:45]); surgery downtime of a year to a year and a half (z_6M5r7031A [14:45]). The follow-on question he poses: "How do we know who can benefit from surgery and who won't?" (z_6M5r7031A [15:15]), which he says is mostly clinical decision-making.
19	
20	**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the season count itself: a failed trial moves the operation later. Inference: because the cost is measured in lost seasons, the timing of the injury within the calendar matters, which fits his own point that spring training and the weeks before the playoffs are different injuries (z_6M5r7031A [16:16]).
21	
22	**When to apply** — In any conversation where "try rehab first" is proposed for an injury that might still need surgery, to make the failure branch visible to coaches and athletes. Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine on return to performance and is not stated as the decision-maker (Explicit, Playbook p.6). Inference: the heuristic frames the question to ask Athletic Medicine; it does not answer it.
23	
24	**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the success ranges are given without sources and the caption for the surgery range is garbled. The speaker's context is one UCL injury in professional pitchers, where a "season" is a fixed competitive calendar. The heuristic says nothing about injuries where conservative care is the standard first step. Not a basis for recommending surgery. The speaker says the choice is clinical.
25	
26	**Example** — The speaker's own: non-operative treatment tried first fails, and the pitcher "lost two" seasons instead of one (z_6M5r7031A [15:15]).
27	
28	**Related** — [[framework--expected-value-decision-analysis-for-treatment-choice]] (the model that puts a number on the failure branch).

175	# Use On-Field Athleticism as a Time-Varying Alternative to One Combine Number
176	
177	**What it is** — Eric Eager (PFF) says it is "a little bit silly" that one measurement of a player's athleticism is taken and then used "forever" as his evaluation (Q3i3FOC-dPE [08:49], [09:19]). His point: expected pressure rate, a tracking-based measure of how fast a rusher leaves the ball, tracks athletic measures from the combine or pro day better than the charted data do, so combining the two datasets gives a time-varying athleticism measure for a pass rusher (Q3i3FOC-dPE [09:19], [09:50]). The captions name jump and three-cone measures and say slower players are worse at the first-step measure; the speed measure itself is not named at that point (Q3i3FOC-dPE [09:50]). In Q&A, a questioner reads a correlation of "like 0.75" between 40-yard dash and career pressure rate, and Eager answers "yep"; he explains it uses career averages because "players only test once" (Q3i3FOC-dPE [23:01], [23:31]).
178	
179	**Why it works** — The speaker's stated reason is that an on-field measure is repeated across the career while the test happens once (Q3i3FOC-dPE [08:49], [23:01]). He gives no mechanism beyond that. Inference: a repeated measure can show change over time; a single test cannot.
180	
181	**When to apply** — When a one-time test (combine, camp, pre-season) is being used as a long-lived label. Eric's baseline: weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent testing so plateaus and declines are caught early (Inferred, course-team position, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: this talk extends that direction using in-play data.
182	
183	**When NOT to apply** — The 0.75 is a questioner's reading of a slide, not a number the captions confirm; it uses career averages versus a one-time test, not within-player prediction (Q3i3FOC-dPE [23:01], [23:31]). `untested`: no values are in the captions. The NFL data are league-wide shoulder-pad tracking; Baylor sees only its own sensors and no opponent comparison group. Not evidence that the 40 is useless; the speaker says players who do well on the field "generally" do well at the combine (Q3i3FOC-dPE [14:25]).
184	
185	**Example** — The speaker's: the three-cone and jump panels, each tracking the on-field measure (Q3i3FOC-dPE [09:50]).
186	
187	**Related** — [[framework--charted-grades-as-labels-tracking-data-as-predictors]], [[case-study--speed-adjusted-receiver-grade-landry-kupp-brown]].

407	
408	# Credit Pass-Rush Pressure Across the Whole Play, Not Only the Final Event
409	
410	**What it is** — Hong's starting point: pass-rush statistics record only the outcome (sack, and counts of hits and hurries), so a rusher who closes on the quarterback but does not finish gets no credit (1nt8hK2oYrE [01:02], [01:34], [02:05]). The aim is to measure pressure "continuously applied throughout a play" and give credit to the defensive players who apply it (1nt8hK2oYrE [01:02], [02:38]). Outputs the speaker names: how long the passer is under pressure, and a "pressure zone", time with the score above 75 percent (1nt8hK2oYrE [14:34]).
411	
412	In the example plays, three players generate high pressure, two early and one later who gets the sack (1nt8hK2oYrE [13:00]), and in another the model credits two players with forcing the passer out of the pocket where "a human label" credited one (1nt8hK2oYrE [14:04]).
413	
414	**Why it works** — The speaker gives no evidence the continuous credit is more accurate than the human label, only that it differs on his examples. Inference: counting outcomes only discards the time and path information that tracking data hold.
415	
416	**When to apply** — When a coach's question is about a process that unfolds over a play and the available statistic records one endpoint. Ask whether tracking or film data can record the path, and who would act on it.
417	
418	Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." (Eric-authored SportSmith, in method-baseline.md.) Inference: finer-grained credit is worth collecting only if it changes a decision about a player, and the talk reports no decision outcome.
419	
420	**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: the evidence is two sample plays and no accuracy for the score itself (see [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]). It is NFL data and ignores scheme, double teams and stunts as credit modifiers (1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]). The speaker's own Q&A answers confirm the score does not say whose pressure it is (1nt8hK2oYrE [21:40]), so using it to rank individual rushers goes beyond what the talk shows. One panel questioner argued the metric should weight how early pressure arrives (a hurry at 3 seconds beats one at 5.5), and the speaker agreed it was a good point (1nt8hK2oYrE [19:38], [20:09]).
421	
422	**Example** — The speaker's: a play where two rushers create high pressure early and a third late "who eventually get the sack" (1nt8hK2oYrE [13:00]).
423	
424	**Related** — [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-three-stage-pipeline]]; [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]. Contrast with [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]] (SSAC25), which argues about what a credited number can mean and applies to this kind of per-player credit.
